title: Arepas Colombianas
subtitle: Thick griddled corn flatbreads, plain or filled with cheese
excerpt: Thick, soft corn flatbreads cooked on a hot griddle until golden on both sides. This recipe makes 8 arepas and takes about 30 minutes. They are a daily staple in Colombia, eaten at breakfast with butter and cheese or served alongside main meals in place of bread.
sourceNotes: Arepas predate Spanish colonisation and were eaten by the indigenous Timoto-Cuica people of present-day Venezuela and Colombia. They remain a daily staple across Colombia, eaten for breakfast, lunch and supper. Colombian arepas are thicker and plainer than Venezuelan ones, and are often spread with butter or stuffed with cheese.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze cooked and cooled arepas between sheets of baking paper. Reheat on a dry griddle for 4 to 5 minutes each side.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch and freeze. Reheat individually as needed.

content.text: This recipe makes 8 arepas and takes about 30 minutes from start to plate. The dough comes together very quickly: mix, shape and cook on a hot griddle. Colombian arepas are thicker than the Venezuelan version, about 1.5cm thick, and have a mild flavour that works with both sweet and savoury toppings.

The only flour that works for arepas is masa harina, a pre-cooked corn flour sold in Latin American shops and many large supermarkets. Do not use polenta, regular cornmeal or corn flour (cornstarch): none of these will produce the right texture. Add the water gradually as the exact amount depends on the brand of masa harina. The dough should be smooth, slightly tacky and hold its shape when pressed into a patty without cracking at the edges.

Combine the masa harina and 1 tsp salt in a large bowl. Add the melted butter and 300ml warm water, mixing as you go. The dough should come together into a smooth, non-sticky mass. If it cracks when pressed, add more water a tablespoon at a time.
If adding cheese, mix 100g finely grated mozzarella or mild white cheese into the dough now.
Divide the dough into 8 equal balls. Press each one between your palms into a flat disc about 1.5cm thick and 8 to 9cm in diameter. Smooth any cracks at the edges with damp fingers.

Heat a griddle pan or heavy frying pan over medium heat. Brush with a little oil. Cook the arepas in batches for 5 to 6 minutes on each side until the surface is golden with some darker spots and the arepa sounds hollow when tapped.
Serve warm with butter, sliced avocado, fresh cheese or alongside a main meal. Arepas are best eaten the day they are made but can be reheated in a dry pan.

attrs.symptom: Arepas are cracking around the edges
attrs.fix: Add warm water a tablespoon at a time and knead it in until the dough is smooth and pliable. The dough should feel slightly tacky but not sticky.

attrs.symptom: Arepas are burning outside but still raw inside
attrs.fix: Use medium heat throughout. Arepas need time to cook through. If the outside is colouring too fast, reduce the heat and cover loosely with foil.

attrs.cause: Dough was compacted too firmly when shaping, or too much water was added
attrs.fix: Handle the dough gently and shape with light pressure. The dough should feel soft, not solid. Too much water makes the dough heavy and the arepa dense.

content.text: Arepas are eaten three times a day in Colombian households, which is rarer than it sounds. They are on the breakfast table, sold hot from street carts at lunchtime and served alongside the evening meal. In Bogota the plain arepa is popular, spread with butter and a slice of white cheese. In the Valle del Cauca region, the arepa de choclo is made from sweet fresh corn. Each region has a style it considers the correct one.
